title: Tanzanian Boiled Cassava
community: Enjoyed nationwide — particularly coastal and western Tanzania
author: Mama Salima
desc: Mihogo ya Kuchemsha — cassava boiled in salted water until completely tender, served with a pinch of salt, pili pili sauce, or a drizzle of coconut cream. The simple, filling, everyday snack and side dish of Tanzania — available at every roadside stall.
longDesc: Boiled cassava is one of Tanzania's most widely eaten foods — affordable, filling, and available everywhere. It is eaten as a morning snack, a lunch side, and a between-meal filler. Served with pili pili or coconut cream, it transcends its simplicity.
ingredients: 600g fresh cassava — peeled and cut into chunks
Pili pili sauce or coconut cream to serve
steps: Peel cassava and remove the woody central fibre. Cut into chunks.
Place in a pot with cold salted water.
Bring to a boil. Cook for 20—25 minutes until completely tender.
Drain and serve with pili pili sauce or coconut cream.
chefTips: Remove the woody central fibre completely — it does not soften during cooking.
Cassava is done when a fork slides in without resistance.
Fresh cassava is vastly better than frozen.
cookingScience: Cassava must be properly cooked — raw cassava contains linamarin, a cyanogenic compound that breaks down harmlessly during cooking and draining. Properly boiled and drained cassava is completely safe to eat.
sustainabilityTips: Cassava is one of the most drought-resistant crops in Tanzania.
culturalNote: Boiled cassava is the affordable, reliable staple that has sustained Tanzanian communities through droughts and lean seasons for generations — cassava's drought resistance has saved lives across East Africa.
